I'm building a new shared repository called Maestro (https://github.com/wp-media/maestro), 
already cloned at /Users/gaelrobin/Desktop/Work/maestro (currently just has a README.md).

## What Maestro is

Maestro is the shared AI delivery pipeline for wp-media's three WordPress plugin projects:
- WP Rocket: /Users/gaelrobin/LocalSites/wpmedia/app/public/wp-content/plugins/wp-rocket
- Imagify: /Users/gaelrobin/Desktop/Work/imagify-plugin
- BackWPup: /Users/gaelrobin/Local Sites/bwu/app/public/wp-content/plugins/backwpup-pro

Each project currently has its own copy of the pipeline in `.aiassistant/` — agents, 
skills, orchestrator. They've diverged significantly (WP Rocket is the most advanced, 
Imagify is furthest behind). Maestro solves this by being the single source of truth 
that all three projects pull from.

## Architecture decision (already made)

The agents are ~95% identical across projects. The only differences are a handful of 
project-specific strings (slug in paths, architecture skill name, repo name, etc.). 
BackWPup and Imagify already have a `config/repo-map.json` describing their structure. 
WP Rocket doesn't have one yet.

The solution: add an `ai` section to `repo-map.json` in each project, and update agents 
to read from it instead of hardcoding project-specific values. Agents become fully 
config-driven. Maestro holds the agents; projects hold their config.

## repo-map.json `ai` section (to be designed)

Needs to capture at minimum:
- slug (used in TemporaryItems paths, e.g. "wp-rocket", "backwpup", "imagify-plugin")
- repo (e.g. "wp-media/wp-rocket")
- temp_root (e.g. ".TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket")
- architecture_skill (e.g. "wp-rocket-architecture")
- frontend_skill (e.g. "wp-rocket-frontend-architecture")
- editions (e.g. ["free","pro"] for BackWPup, omitted for others)
- Any other project-specific values agents currently hardcode

## Source of truth for agents

Use WP Rocket's branch `chore/ai-orchestration-improvements` as the source — it's the 
most advanced version, includes all workshop feedback fixes. Key files to port:
- .aiassistant/agents/ (all agents)
- .aiassistant/skills/ EXCEPT wp-rocket-architecture/ and wp-rocket-frontend-architecture/ 
  (those stay in wp-rocket)
- .aiassistant/specs/phpcs/ (shared across all 3, all WP plugins)
- .aiassistant/skills/orchestrator/
- .aiassistant/skills/dod/
- .aiassistant/skills/e2e/
- .aiassistant/skills/docs/
- .aiassistant/skills/knowledge-graph/
- .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/ (including scripts/)
- .aiassistant/skills/wordpress-compliance/

## What stays per-project (NOT in Maestro)

- config/repo-map.json (project identity + ai config)
- .aiassistant/skills/<project>-architecture/SKILL.md
- .aiassistant/skills/<project>-frontend-architecture/SKILL.md
- .aiassistant/graph/dependency-graph.json (auto-generated)
- .aiassistant/skills/orchestrator/html-log-format.md (already in WP Rocket — keep in Maestro)

## What needs to be built in Maestro

1. The full `.aiassistant/` directory structure (ported from WP Rocket's branch, 
   agents made config-driven)
2. A `.template/repo-map.json` showing the full schema including the `ai` section
3. A `bin/sync-pipeline.sh` script each project runs to pull updates from Maestro 
   (must never overwrite config/, project-specific skills/, or graph/)
4. An `AGENTS.md` base file (project-specific sections like Session Learnings stay 
   in each project)
5. README.md — description: "One baton, many orchestras. Maestro holds the agents, 
   skills, and orchestration logic that every wp-media plugin project plays from — 
   each tuned to its own codebase, all moving in sync."

## Key design constraints

- Agents must read `.aiassistant/config/repo-map.json` at startup — no hardcoded 
  project names/slugs/paths anywhere in agents
- The sync script must be safe to re-run (idempotent) and must protect project-specific files
- BackWPup has a Free/Pro edition split — agents need to handle `editions` from 
  repo-map.json when present (affects scope assignment and review rules)
- Imagify has E2E tests as part of CI (unique to that project) — this should be 
  expressible via repo-map.json config, not a fork of the e2e skill

## What to do first

Start by reading the source files from WP Rocket's branch to understand the current 
state, then design the exact `repo-map.json` `ai` schema, then build out Maestro's 
directory structure with config-driven agents.

The working directory for this task is /Users/gaelrobin/Desktop/Work/maestro



```
Hardcoded strings to make config-driven (already identified):
```

`- "wp-rocket" / "backwpup" / "imagify-plugin" in TemporaryItems paths → repo-map.ai.slug`
`- "wp-rocket-architecture" skill name → repo-map.ai.architecture_skill`
`- "wp-media/wp-rocket" repo reference → repo-map.repo`
`- "/wp-json/wp-rocket/v1/" REST namespace → repo-map.ai.rest_namespace`
`- "github-manager" vs "release-agent" (BackWPup is on old arch) → repo-map.ai.push_agent`
`- "WP Rocket" plugin name in prose → repo-map.name`

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- agents-observe:observe: Agents Observe dashboard and server management
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

### 4. **frontend-agent.md**

**Pipeline structure:**
- Step 1: Issue read → extract acceptance criteria
- Step 2: Grooming (always runs)
- Step 3: Post-grooming routing → complexity signal assessment, model routing
- Step 3a: Handle open_questions and NTH items

- Step 6: Release agent (push & PR creation)
- Steps 7–9: Quality gates (DOD L2, Lead Review, QA)
- Step 11: Finalize (update PR body, move out of draft, post summary)

.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issue-<N>/
├── tasks.json               # shared task ledger
├── contracts/
│   ├── backend-api.json     # hooks, option_keys, rest_endpoints (written by backend-agent)

│   └── frontend-result.json # frontend completion result

- Must return PASS or WARN before handoff (FAILs self-corrected)

**Layer 2** (orchestrator independent gate):
- Runs after PR is open
- Can return PASS, WARN, or FAIL
- Provides layer1_delta (issues L2 caught that L1 missed)

**5 Checks:**
1. Manual validation — "What was tested" section non-empty and specific
2. Automated tests — tests exist and pass for all changed source files
3. Documentation — public API changes documented (hooks, options, routes, capabilities)
4. PR description — all template sections filled and non-empty
5. CI — local PHPCS/PHPStan/tests (L1) or remote GitHub Actions checks (L2)

WordPress.org and repository PHPCS compliance:

- Every new filter → wpm_apply_filters_typed() (never apply_filters)
- Plugin settings → injected Options_Data (never get_option)

```
inc/Engine/MyFeature/
├── ServiceProvider.php       # binds all services
├── Context/Context.php       # is this feature active?
├── Admin/Subscriber.php      # admin-only hooks
├── Frontend/
│   ├── Controller.php        # business logic

    ├── Rows/MyFeature.php
    └── Schemas/MyFeature.php

### 3. AGENTS: Full Content (10 Agent Definitions)

All agent files are located in `.aiassistant/agents/`:

#### A. orchestrator.md

Adaptive central coordinator for the issue workflow. Does not write code. Coordinates all pipeline steps: grooming → challenger review → implementation → E2E suite → lead review → push/PR → CI → QA → finalization.

**Key responsibilities:**
- Read issue and extract acceptance criteria
- Invoke grooming-agent
- Route based on grooming JSON (effort, risk, complexity)
- Conditionally invoke challenger for complex/risky issues
- Manage implementation agents (backend/frontend) with max 3 attempts each
- Run E2E suite always after implementation
- Invoke release-agent for PR creation
- Run DOD L2 gate (composer test-unit, composer phpcs-changed)
- Invoke lead-reviewer conditionally
- Monitor CI checks with ci-agent
- Invoke qa-engineer conditionally
- Finalize PR and post summary comment

**Detailed JSON contracts** for all agent return types (grooming, challenger, implementation, release, DOD L2, lead review, QA).

**HTML log format** with event types (decision, agent, gate, escalation, parallel) and color-coded visualization.

#### B. lead-reviewer.md

Lead software engineer code review agent. Reviews git diff against implementation spec and project standards. Invoked after PR is opened in draft state.

**Process:**
1. Read implementation spec from `.TemporaryItems/Issues/imagify-plugin/issues/<N>-spec.md`
2. Get changed files: `git diff <base-branch> --name-only`
3. Read each changed file in full
4. Review against spec's Implementation Plan, Edge Cases, Tests Required, Out of Scope
5. Review against project standards (architecture, tests, general code quality)
6. Load skill files: `imagify-architecture/SKILL.md` and `wordpress-compliance/SKILL.md`
7. Classify findings (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW)
8. Post inline comments for CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM findings to PR
9. Return JSON with verdict (PASS or REQUEST_CHANGES), blockers, and nice_to_haves

#### C. backend-agent.md

Backend implementation agent. Implements PHP changes following spec and dispatch plan. Writes/updates unit tests. Runs PHPCS and static analysis before committing.

**Process:**
1. Load context: read spec, dispatch plan, architecture skills
2. Implement backend-only changes in `classes/` with strict types
3. Follow TDD: write tests alongside implementation
4. Run DOD L1: `composer test-unit` and `composer phpcs-changed`
5. Self-correct all failures before committing
6. Commit with one atomic commit and `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>` trailer
7. Return JSON with ticket_id, branch, files_changed, tests_passing, dod_layer1 results

#### D. qa-engineer.md

Quality Assurance agent. Validates PR against ticket spec using strategy selection (API, Browser, Analysis). Invoked after PR opens or when testing PR.

**Process:**
1. Deploy PR branch: `gh pr checkout <N>` and `bash bin/dev-up.sh --no-seed`
2. Gather context: ticket spec, changed files, full file content, PR diff
3. Determine validation strategies: API/functional, Browser/UI (delegates to e2e-qa-tester), Analysis fallback
4. Execute each strategy with concrete evidence
5. Run smoke tests (settings page, bulk optimization, media library column, plugin activation)
6. Write new tests for uncovered acceptance criteria
7. Generate test report with AC results and smoke test results
8. Post report as PR comment
9. Return JSON with overall (PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL), criteria_results, smoke_tests, blockers, recommendations

#### E. challenger.md

Adversarial spec reviewer. Challenges grooming spec for complex/high-risk issues. Finds hidden risks, unvalidated assumptions, missing dependencies.

**Process:**
1. Read issue file and spec file in full
2. Challenge from 6 angles: root cause, hidden assumptions, missing dependencies, effort realism, scope/risk, alternatives
3. Classify findings (MUST_HAVE, SHOULD_HAVE, COULD_HAVE, NICE_TO_HAVE)
4. Produce verdict: APPROVED, NEEDS_REVISION, or BLOCKED
5. Post challenge report as GitHub issue comment
6. Return JSON with plan_version, verdict, feedback array, alternative_suggestions, revised_risk_level

#### F. e2e-qa-tester.md

Imagify QA engineer specialized in end-to-end testing. Boots wp-env, drives WordPress admin via Playwright, converts validated flows to Playwright specs.

**Environment:**
- Local URL: `http://localhost:8888`
- Admin: `admin` / `password`
- Boot: `bash bin/dev-up.sh` (idempotent)
- Seed: `bash bin/dev-seed.sh`
- Screenshot root: `.e2e-screenshots/`
- Test files: `tests/e2e/`

**Process:**
1. Get context: read PR's "How to test" section, linked issue, changed files (full)
2. Bring up environment with seed
3. Drive flow manually with Playwright MCP
4. Take screenshots at checkpoints
5. Publish screenshots to GitHub (commit SHA-based URLs)
6. Convert validated flow into deterministic Playwright tests
7. Use Page Object Model (SettingsPage, BulkOptimizationPage, MediaLibraryPage)
8. Guard API-dependent tests with `test.skip` for `IMAGIFY_TESTS_API_KEY`
9. Return test report with screenshots and Playwright test files committed

#### G. ci-agent.md

CI monitoring agent. Reads GitHub Actions workflows, monitors PR checks, reports ALL_PASS, FAILURE, or TIMEOUT.

**Process:**
1. Detect repository (if not provided)
2. Enumerate CI checks from `.github/workflows/*.yml` matching `pull_request` trigger
3. Poll `gh pr checks <pr_number>` every 60 seconds until all pass/fail or 20 min timeout
4. On failure, extract job log: `gh run view <run_id> --log-failed`
5. Identify root cause from relevant error lines
6. Return formatted report with check results and error excerpts

#### H. frontend-agent.md

Frontend implementation agent. Implements JS/CSS/HTML changes following spec and dispatch plan. Runs JS linting.

**Process:**
1. Load context: spec, dispatch plan, frontend architecture skills
2. Implement frontend-only (no PHP), follow spec's Implementation Plan
3. Core rules: no jQuery, no inline event handlers, no unsafe innerHTML, localized nonces
4. Run DOD L1: `npm run lint` and `npm run build`
5. Self-correct all failures before committing
6. Commit one atomic commit with `Co-Authored-By` trailer
7. Return JSON with ticket_id, branch, files_changed, tests_passing, dod_layer1 results

#### I. grooming-agent.md

Issue grooming agent. Analyzes GitHub issue in depth, maps affected codebase, determines architecturally correct solution, produces implementation spec.

**Process:**
1. Read issue file (and parent epic if exists)
2. Map affected code: identify classes, methods, hooks, subscribers, modules; read each file in full; trace call chains; identify related tests
3. Architectural analysis: root-cause vs workaround? Where does fix belong? Edge cases?
4. Write implementation spec to `.TemporaryItems/Issues/imagify-plugin/issues/<N>-spec.md`
5. Post grooming plan as comment on issue
6. Return JSON with ticket_id, relevant_files, approach, development_steps, test_plan, risks, effort, complexity, risk_level, risk_notes, grooming_confidence, open_questions

Effort calibration:
- XS: ≤1 file, trivial
- S: 2–3 files, no new patterns
- M: 3–6 files, new class/interface
- L: 7–10 files, architectural shift
- XL: 10+ files or new module

#### J. release-agent.md

Push branch to remote and create GitHub pull request. Does not write code. Invoked after lead-reviewer returns PASS.

**Process:**
1. Push: `git push -u origin <branch>`
2. Initialize PR draft: `bash .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/scripts/init-pr-draft.sh <N>`
3. Fill PR draft with title, "What was done", "How to test", "Type of change"
4. Create PR with `gh pr create`
5. Assign and label: `gh pr edit <PR_number> --add-assignee @me --add-label "Made by AI"`
6. Return PR number, URL, branch pushed status

### 4. SKILLS: Full Content (5 Skills with Supporting Files)

All skills located in `.aiassistant/skills/`:

#### A. imagify-architecture/SKILL.md

Use when changing service structure, shared logic, bootstrapping, dependency wiring, or adding new classes.

**Core principles:**
- New features in `classes/` with `Imagify\` namespace
- `inc/classes/` is legacy — do not add there; migrate out instead
- `declare(strict_types=1)` required on all new `classes/` files
- No new `InstanceGetterTrait` / fake singletons in `classes/`
- No global state or static helpers replacing services
- No tight coupling between UI and infrastructure

**DI rules:**
- Wire through `Imagify\Dependencies\League\Container\Container`
- Register in relevant `ServiceProvider` under `classes/*/ServiceProvider.php`
- List subscribers in `ServiceProvider::get_subscribers()`
- Add providers to `config/providers.php`

**Structural expectations:**
- Service provider pattern
- Subscriber pattern (SubscriberInterface)
- Container-based wiring (no `new` in business logic)
- Strict types in `classes/`

**Avoid:**
- New singletons or `InstanceGetterTrait` in new code
- `get_instance()` patterns in `classes/`
- Direct superglobal access inside services
- Static helpers replacing services

**Legacy migration:**
- Prefer moving class to `classes/` if change is substantial
- Quick fix: fix in place without expanding legacy patterns
- Deprecated classes/traits: move to `inc/deprecated/`, never delete

#### B. knowledge-graph/SKILL.md

Use to understand repository structure, trace class dependencies, find symbol's file, explore module relationships without re-scanning codebase.

**Graph shape at `.aiassistant/graph/dependency-graph.json`:**
- `generated_at`: ISO timestamp
- `base_commit`: git SHA when built
- `node_count`: total files scanned
- `nodes`: keyed by relative file path, each with language, namespace (PHP), symbols, imports
- `symbol_index`: maps FQN class/interface/trait/enum to file path

**How to use:**
- Find class file: `symbol_index["Imagify\\Optimization\\Process\\AbstractProcess"]`
- List classes in namespace: filter `nodes` where `namespace` starts with `Imagify\Media`
- Trace dependencies: read `nodes["path/to/file.php"].imports`
- Find importers: search `nodes[*].imports` for target FQN

**Keeping fresh:**
- Record base_commit; if differs from HEAD, run: `node bin/build-knowledge-graph.js`
- Use `--full` to force complete rebuild
- Incremental by default (only re-parses changed files since base_commit)

**Supported languages:**
- PHP: namespace, class/interface/trait/enum declarations, use imports (including grouped `\{A, B}`)
- TypeScript/JavaScript: static + dynamic imports and require() sources

#### C. wordpress-compliance/SKILL.md

Use when modifying templates, admin UI, output, hooks, plugin metadata, sanitization, escaping, or any code for WordPress.org compliance.

**Ensure compatibility with:**
- WordPress Plugin Check
- Repository PHPCS rules
- WordPress.org expectations

**Responsibilities:**
- Respect repository PHPCS configuration
- Follow WordPress escaping standards
- Avoid forbidden or deprecated APIs
- Avoid direct superglobal access without sanitization
- Ensure output escaped for context

**Escaping heuristics:**
- HTML text: `esc_html()`
- HTML attribute: `esc_attr()`
- URL: `esc_url()`
- Allowed HTML: `wp_kses_post()`

**JavaScript:**
- Do not use jQuery; use native DOM APIs (document.querySelector, addEventListener, fetch, etc.)

**Anti-patterns:**
- Echoing raw variables
- Introducing unescaped output
- Storing sensitive values in plain text
- Bypassing repository PHPCS configuration
- Using jQuery in new/modified JS

**Related specs:** `.aiassistant/specs/phpcs/` for recurring technical problems

#### D. imagify-frontend-architecture/SKILL.md

Use when changing admin JavaScript, CSS, or HTML templates.

**Core principles:**
- No jQuery — native DOM APIs only
- No inline event handlers (`onclick`, `onchange`, etc.) — use `addEventListener`
- No unsafe `innerHTML` — use `textContent` or `createElement`/`appendChild`
- Remove event listeners on teardown to avoid memory leaks

**Admin UI areas:**
- Settings page: `assets/js/` and `assets/css/`
- Media library column: must not interfere with core behavior
- Bulk optimization: AJAX-driven; always show progress; handle errors visibly

**AJAX/REST:**
- Use native `fetch` with localized nonce
- Always handle errors explicitly (show feedback, never fail silently)
- Nonces via `wp_localize_script` — never hardcoded

**Structural expectations:**
- New JS entry points registered + enqueued through Subscriber
- No new global variables — use data attributes or module patterns
- E2E tests for new UI flows in `tests/e2e/` — update alongside implementation

### 5. SPECS: PHPCS Compliance Specifications

All specs at `.aiassistant/specs/phpcs/`:

#### A. escaped-output.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.EscapeOutput.OutputNotEscaped

**Goal:** Ensure all HTML output is escaped in correct context, reducing PHPCS warnings and preventing XSS.

**Scope:** Templates and PHP using `echo`, `print`, `printf` in `views/`, `inc/`, `classes/`.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map all output points
2. Reuse existing patterns: `esc_html__`, `esc_html_e`, `esc_attr__`, `esc_attr_e`, `esc_html()`, `esc_attr()`, `esc_url()`, `wp_kses()`, `wp_kses_post()`
3. When translated string contains HTML, use `wp_kses()` with allowlist

**Decision by context:**
- HTML text: `esc_html()`
- HTML attribute/data-*: `esc_attr()`
- URL: `esc_url()`
- Inline JS: `esc_js()` or `wp_json_encode()` + `esc_attr()`
- Allowed HTML: `wp_kses_post()` or `wp_kses($html, $allowed_html)`

**Implementation patterns:**
- Escape at output boundary, not source
- Use pre-escaped translation helpers
- For printf/sprintf, escape each variable before injecting
- Avoid raw `echo $html`; use `wp_kses` with explicit allowlist
- Do not double-escape if already escaped
- Do not use `echo esc_html_e()`/`echo esc_attr_e()` (these already echo)
- For dynamic classes/ids: prefer `esc_attr()` or `sanitize_html_class()`

**Examples provided for all patterns above.**

#### B. nonce-verification-recommended.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.NonceVerification.Recommended

**Goal:** Ensure any request data processing in admin/UI includes proper nonce verification. When flow is not user-driven (cron, webhooks, external), apply equivalent auth/validation.

**Scope:** Files in `inc/` and `classes/` emitting `WordPress.Security.NonceVerification.Recommended`.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map existing patterns with search for `check_admin_referer`, `wp_verify_nonce`, `wp_nonce_field`
2. Reuse screen's existing action/field
3. If no helper fits, create private method in class
4. Do not invent new action if screen already uses one (keep DRY)

**Out of scope:**
- Do not add `phpcs:ignore` by default
- Do not change public endpoint behavior without validating integration impact

**Decision (quick tree):**
1. Is it a user action on admin screen? Yes → add required nonce. No → go to 2.
2. Is it cron/CLI/external endpoint with own auth (token/secret)? Yes → validate mechanism and document why nonce doesn't apply. No → re-evaluate.

**Strategy by use type:**
1. Admin forms/actions (POST): Add `wp_nonce_field()` in form; call `check_admin_referer()` before reading data; always `wp_unslash()` before sanitizing
2. List filters (GET) without side effects: Verify nonce (`wp_verify_nonce`) and only use values when valid
3. Cron/automatic: If existing auth exists, validate explicitly and document. If no auth, propose simple token.

**Implementation patterns with examples for all three types.**

#### C. validated-sanitized-input.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.ValidatedSanitizedInput

**Goal:** Ensure any input from GET/POST/COOKIE/SERVER/REQUEST is unslashed, validated, sanitized before use.

**Scope:** Files in `inc/`, `classes/`, `views/` reading superglobals or external input.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map access to `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_SERVER`
2. Reuse patterns: `sanitize_text_field(wp_unslash($_GET['foo']))`, `sanitize_email(wp_unslash($_POST['email']))`, `absint(wp_unslash($_GET['id']))`, etc.
3. Verify nonces for admin actions (cross-reference to nonce-verification spec)

**Decision (quick tree):**
1. Is input from superglobal? Apply `wp_unslash()`
2. Clear type/allowlist? Validate before use
3. Sanitize with correct function
4. Invalid/missing? Use safe default

**Implementation patterns:**
- MissingUnslash: always `wp_unslash()` before `sanitize_*`
- InputNotSanitized: apply `sanitize_*` or `esc_url_raw()`
- InputNotValidated: validate with allowlist, `absint`, `filter_var()`, controlled regex
- Prefer `filter_input()`/`filter_input_array()` with `FILTER_SANITIZE_*`
- If `filter_input()` returns null but superglobal set, fall back to `sanitize_text_field(wp_unslash(...))`
- Avoid `$_REQUEST`; prefer `$_GET` or `$_POST`
- For arrays: sanitize each with `array_map`
- For URLs: `esc_url_raw()` + optionally `filter_var(..., FILTER_VALIDATE_URL)`
- For multiline text: `sanitize_textarea_field()` (not `sanitize_text_field`)
- For allowed HTML: `wp_kses_post()` (only when needed/documented)
- For boolean flags: `filter_input(INPUT_POST, 'flag', FILTER_VALIDATE_BOOLEAN)` or `(bool) filter_input(...)`
- For filters/ordering (GET): validate nonce and allowlist

**Examples for all patterns and verification steps.**

## Complete Survey: .aiassistant/ and config/ Directories

### Directory Structure Overview

The Imagify plugin repository contains a comprehensive AI assistant configuration under `.aiassistant/` with the following structure:

```
.aiassistant/
├── agents/              (10 agent definitions)

## COMPLETE FILE CONTENTS

### 1. AGENTS.MD (Project Root)

**File:** `/Users/gaelrobin/Desktop/Work/imagify-plugin/AGENTS.md`

This is the mandatory guardrail document for ALL AI-assisted work. Key sections:

- **Project Overview:** Single-edition WordPress plugin (no FREE/PRO split). PSR-4 modern code in `classes/` with `Imagify\` namespace; legacy code in `inc/classes/` being migrated out.
- **Technology Stack:** PHP 7.3+, WordPress plugin APIs, League Container (DI), ActionScheduler, Strauss, JavaScript/Grunt, Playwright E2E tests
- **Code Structure:** Modern code goes in `classes/`, legacy in `inc/classes/`, frontend in `_dev/`, tests in `Tests/` and `Tests/e2e/`
- **Coding Standards:** PHPCS rules, PHPStan, WordPress Plugin Check compliance required
- **Architectural Integrity:** No global state, no new singletons in `classes/`, strict DI patterns, no new `inc/classes/` additions
- **Testing & Validation:** Each change must pass PHPCS, static analysis, avoid altering unrelated tests
- **E2E Testing:** Two Claude Code sub-agents: `qa-engineer` and `e2e-qa-tester`
- **Local Development:** wp-env Docker setup with `bash bin/dev-up.sh`, `bin/dev-down.sh`, `bin/dev-seed.sh`, `bin/test-e2e.sh`
- **Git Commit Policy:** AI may only suggest commits by default. Exception: Issue Workflow agents may run `git commit` and `git push` atomically.
- **PR Hygiene:** Minimal, scoped changes; clear intent; no noise in diff
- **Security First:** User input untrusted, no plain-text sensitive values, no unsafe serialization, escape unescaped output
- **Sub-Agents:** `qa-engineer` and `e2e-qa-tester` in `.aiassistant/agents/`
- **Skills Activation:** Use relevant skills per task type (template changes → WordPress Compliance, structural → Imagify Architecture, etc.)

### 3. AGENTS: Full Content (10 Agent Definitions)

All agent files are located in `.aiassistant/agents/`:

#### A. orchestrator.md

Adaptive central coordinator for the issue workflow. Does not write code. Coordinates all pipeline steps: grooming → challenger review → implementation → E2E suite → lead review → push/PR → CI → QA → finalization.

**Key responsibilities:**
- Read issue and extract acceptance criteria
- Invoke grooming-agent
- Route based on grooming JSON (effort, risk, complexity)
- Conditionally invoke challenger for complex/risky issues
- Manage implementation agents (backend/frontend) with max 3 attempts each
- Run E2E suite always after implementation
- Invoke release-agent for PR creation
- Run DOD L2 gate (composer test-unit, composer phpcs-changed)
- Invoke lead-reviewer conditionally
- Monitor CI checks with ci-agent
- Invoke qa-engineer conditionally
- Finalize PR and post summary comment

**Detailed JSON contracts** for all agent return types (grooming, challenger, implementation, release, DOD L2, lead review, QA).

**HTML log format** with event types (decision, agent, gate, escalation, parallel) and color-coded visualization.

#### B. lead-reviewer.md

Lead software engineer code review agent. Reviews git diff against implementation spec and project standards. Invoked after PR is opened in draft state.

**Process:**
1. Read implementation spec from `.TemporaryItems/Issues/imagify-plugin/issues/<N>-spec.md`
2. Get changed files: `git diff <base-branch> --name-only`
3. Read each changed file in full
4. Review against spec's Implementation Plan, Edge Cases, Tests Required, Out of Scope
5. Review against project standards (architecture, tests, general code quality)
6. Load skill files: `imagify-architecture/SKILL.md` and `wordpress-compliance/SKILL.md`
7. Classify findings (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW)
8. Post inline comments for CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM findings to PR
9. Return JSON with verdict (PASS or REQUEST_CHANGES), blockers, and nice_to_haves

#### C. backend-agent.md

Backend implementation agent. Implements PHP changes following spec and dispatch plan. Writes/updates unit tests. Runs PHPCS and static analysis before committing.

**Process:**
1. Load context: read spec, dispatch plan, architecture skills
2. Implement backend-only changes in `classes/` with strict types
3. Follow TDD: write tests alongside implementation
4. Run DOD L1: `composer test-unit` and `composer phpcs-changed`
5. Self-correct all failures before committing
6. Commit with one atomic commit and `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>` trailer
7. Return JSON with ticket_id, branch, files_changed, tests_passing, dod_layer1 results

#### D. qa-engineer.md

Quality Assurance agent. Validates PR against ticket spec using strategy selection (API, Browser, Analysis). Invoked after PR opens or when testing PR.

**Process:**
1. Deploy PR branch: `gh pr checkout <N>` and `bash bin/dev-up.sh --no-seed`
2. Gather context: ticket spec, changed files, full file content, PR diff
3. Determine validation strategies: API/functional, Browser/UI (delegates to e2e-qa-tester), Analysis fallback
4. Execute each strategy with concrete evidence
5. Run smoke tests (settings page, bulk optimization, media library column, plugin activation)
6. Write new tests for uncovered acceptance criteria
7. Generate test report with AC results and smoke test results
8. Post report as PR comment
9. Return JSON with overall (PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL), criteria_results, smoke_tests, blockers, recommendations

#### E. challenger.md

Adversarial spec reviewer. Challenges grooming spec for complex/high-risk issues. Finds hidden risks, unvalidated assumptions, missing dependencies.

**Process:**
1. Read issue file and spec file in full
2. Challenge from 6 angles: root cause, hidden assumptions, missing dependencies, effort realism, scope/risk, alternatives
3. Classify findings (MUST_HAVE, SHOULD_HAVE, COULD_HAVE, NICE_TO_HAVE)
4. Produce verdict: APPROVED, NEEDS_REVISION, or BLOCKED
5. Post challenge report as GitHub issue comment
6. Return JSON with plan_version, verdict, feedback array, alternative_suggestions, revised_risk_level

#### F. e2e-qa-tester.md

Imagify QA engineer specialized in end-to-end testing. Boots wp-env, drives WordPress admin via Playwright, converts validated flows to Playwright specs.

**Process:**

4. Take screenshots at checkpoints

#### G. ci-agent.md

CI monitoring agent. Reads GitHub Actions workflows, monitors PR checks, reports ALL_PASS, FAILURE, or TIMEOUT.

**Process:**
1. Detect repository (if not provided)
2. Enumerate CI checks from `.github/workflows/*.yml` matching `pull_request` trigger
3. Poll `gh pr checks <pr_number>` every 60 seconds until all pass/fail or 20 min timeout

Issue grooming agent. Analyzes GitHub issue in depth, maps affected codebase, determines architecturally correct solution, produces implementation spec.

**Process:**

Use when changing service structure, shared logic, bootstrapping, dependency wiring, or adding new classes.

- `declare(strict_types=1)` required on all new `classes/` files

- No tight coupling between UI and infrastructure

- List subscribers in `ServiceProvider::get_subscribers()`

**Structural expectations:**
- Service provider pattern
- Subscriber pattern (SubscriberInterface)
- Container-based wiring (no `new` in business logic)
- Strict types in `classes/`

**Avoid:**
- New singletons or `InstanceGetterTrait` in new code
- `get_instance()` patterns in `classes/`
- Direct superglobal access inside services
- Static helpers replacing services

### 5. SPECS: PHPCS Compliance Specifications

All specs at `.aiassistant/specs/phpcs/`:

#### A. escaped-output.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.EscapeOutput.OutputNotEscaped

**Goal:** Ensure all HTML output is escaped in correct context, reducing PHPCS warnings and preventing XSS.

**Scope:** Templates and PHP using `echo`, `print`, `printf` in `views/`, `inc/`, `classes/`.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map all output points
2. Reuse existing patterns: `esc_html__`, `esc_html_e`, `esc_attr__`, `esc_attr_e`, `esc_html()`, `esc_attr()`, `esc_url()`, `wp_kses()`, `wp_kses_post()`
3. When translated string contains HTML, use `wp_kses()` with allowlist

**Decision by context:**
- HTML text: `esc_html()`
- HTML attribute/data-*: `esc_attr()`
- URL: `esc_url()`
- Inline JS: `esc_js()` or `wp_json_encode()` + `esc_attr()`
- Allowed HTML: `wp_kses_post()` or `wp_kses($html, $allowed_html)`

**Implementation patterns:**
- Escape at output boundary, not source
- Use pre-escaped translation helpers
- For printf/sprintf, escape each variable before injecting
- Avoid raw `echo $html`; use `wp_kses` with explicit allowlist
- Do not double-escape if already escaped
- Do not use `echo esc_html_e()`/`echo esc_attr_e()` (these already echo)
- For dynamic classes/ids: prefer `esc_attr()` or `sanitize_html_class()`

**Examples provided for all patterns above.**

#### B. nonce-verification-recommended.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.NonceVerification.Recommended

**Goal:** Ensure any request data processing in admin/UI includes proper nonce verification. When flow is not user-driven (cron, webhooks, external), apply equivalent auth/validation.

**Scope:** Files in `inc/` and `classes/` emitting `WordPress.Security.NonceVerification.Recommended`.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map existing patterns with search for `check_admin_referer`, `wp_verify_nonce`, `wp_nonce_field`
2. Reuse screen's existing action/field
3. If no helper fits, create private method in class
4. Do not invent new action if screen already uses one (keep DRY)

**Out of scope:**
- Do not add `phpcs:ignore` by default
- Do not change public endpoint behavior without validating integration impact

**Decision (quick tree):**
1. Is it a user action on admin screen? Yes → add required nonce. No → go to 2.
2. Is it cron/CLI/external endpoint with own auth (token/secret)? Yes → validate mechanism and document why nonce doesn't apply. No → re-evaluate.

**Strategy by use type:**
1. Admin forms/actions (POST): Add `wp_nonce_field()` in form; call `check_admin_referer()` before reading data; always `wp_unslash()` before sanitizing
2. List filters (GET) without side effects: Verify nonce (`wp_verify_nonce`) and only use values when valid
3. Cron/automatic: If existing auth exists, validate explicitly and document. If no auth, propose simple token.

**Implementation patterns with examples for all three types.**

#### C. validated-sanitized-input.md

SDD: WordPress.Security.ValidatedSanitizedInput

**Goal:** Ensure any input from GET/POST/COOKIE/SERVER/REQUEST is unslashed, validated, sanitized before use.

**Scope:** Files in `inc/`, `classes/`, `views/` reading superglobals or external input.

**Project discovery:**
1. Map access to `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_SERVER`
2. Reuse patterns: `sanitize_text_field(wp_unslash($_GET['foo']))`, `sanitize_email(wp_unslash($_POST['email']))`, `absint(wp_unslash($_GET['id']))`, etc.
3. Verify nonces for admin actions (cross-reference to nonce-verification spec)

**Decision (quick tree):**
1. Is input from superglobal? Apply `wp_unslash()`
2. Clear type/allowlist? Validate before use
3. Sanitize with correct function
4. Invalid/missing? Use safe default

**Implementation patterns:**
- MissingUnslash: always `wp_unslash()` before `sanitize_*`
- InputNotSanitized: apply `sanitize_*` or `esc_url_raw()`
- InputNotValidated: validate with allowlist, `absint`, `filter_var()`, controlled regex
- Prefer `filter_input()`/`filter_input_array()` with `FILTER_SANITIZE_*`
- If `filter_input()` returns null but superglobal set, fall back to `sanitize_text_field(wp_unslash(...))`
- Avoid `$_REQUEST`; prefer `$_GET` or `$_POST`
- For arrays: sanitize each with `array_map`
- For URLs: `esc_url_raw()` + optionally `filter_var(..., FILTER_VALIDATE_URL)`
- For multiline text: `sanitize_textarea_field()` (not `sanitize_text_field`)
- For allowed HTML: `wp_kses_post()` (only when needed/documented)
- For boolean flags: `filter_input(INPUT_POST, 'flag', FILTER_VALIDATE_BOOLEAN)` or `(bool) filter_input(...)`
- For filters/ordering (GET): validate nonce and allowlist

**Examples for all patterns and verification steps.**

8	---
9	
10	# Release Agent
11	
12	You verify commit trailers, push the branch to remote, and create the GitHub pull
13	request. You do not write code. You do not modify implementation files. Two things are
14	unconditional and non-negotiable:
15	
16	1. **Every commit on the branch must include `Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>`**
17	   — verify this before pushing and amend any commit that is missing it.
18	2. **The AI-generated notice must appear at the top of the PR description** — before any
19	   other content, so it is visible without scrolling.
20	
21	## Inputs
22	- Issue number `N`
23	- Branch name
24	- Base branch (e.g. `origin/develop`)
25	- Acceptance criteria list (for the PR body)
26	- Spec path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issues/<N>-spec.md`)
27	- `CURRENT_MODEL` — the model name to use in `Co-Authored-By` trailers (e.g. `Claude Haiku 4.5`)
28	
29	---
30	
31	## Process
32	
33	### Step 1 — Verify `Co-Authored-By` trailer on every commit
34	
35	Before pushing anything, audit the branch:
36	
37	```bash
38	git log <base_branch>..HEAD --format="%H %s" | while read sha msg; do
39	  if ! git show $sha --format="%b" -s | grep -q "Co-Authored-By: Claude"; then
40	    echo "MISSING trailer on $sha: $msg"
41	  fi
42	done
43	```
44	
45	If any commit is missing the trailer, amend it. For the most recent commit:
46	```bash
47	git commit --amend --no-edit --trailer "Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>"
48	```
49	
50	For multiple commits, use a non-interactive rebase with `--exec`:
51	```bash
52	TRAILER="Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>"
53	git rebase <base_branch> --exec \
54	  "git show -s --format='%B' HEAD | grep -q 'Co-Authored-By' || git commit --amend --no-edit --trailer \"$TRAILER\""
55	```
56	
57	`--exec` runs after each commit without opening an editor — safe in automated contexts.
58	
59	After amending, re-run the audit until every commit has the trailer. Set
60	`trailer_verified: true` in the return JSON only after the audit shows zero missing.
61	
62	If any commit on the branch was authored by a human collaborator (not by the agentic
63	pipeline), the trailer is not required on that commit. Identify these by reading the
64	commit author — if it's not `Claude` or `noreply@anthropic.com`, skip the trailer check
65	for that commit and note it in `notes`.
66	
67	---
68	
69	### Step 2 — Push
70	
71	```bash
72	git push -u origin <branch>
73	```
74	
75	If push fails (auth, conflict, protected branch), report the exact error and stop. Do not
76	attempt force-push without explicit instruction.
77

79	
80	### Step 3 — Initialize PR draft
81	
82	```bash
83	bash .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/scripts/init-pr-draft.sh <N>
84	```

87	
88	---
89	
90	### Step 4 — Fill the PR draft
91	
92	Read the spec and the initialized draft. Fill **every section** — no placeholder text
93	left behind.
94	
95	- **The first line of the PR body must be the AI-generated notice:**
96	  ```
97	  > ⚠️ AI-generated — created by an automated pipeline. Review before acting on this.
98	  ```
99	  Prepend it to the draft content. This notice is unconditional — it cannot be omitted,
100	  abbreviated, or moved further down.
101	- Title line: `Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>`. **Never** use conventional-commit
102	  prefix format (`fix(xxx):`, `feat(xxx):`, etc.) in the PR title — that format is for
103	  git commits only.
104	- **Closing keyword line** (mandatory — this is what GitHub uses to link the PR to the issue):
105	  the PR body must contain a standalone line `Closes #<N>` **not** buried in prose. Place it
106	  immediately after the AI-generated notice:
107	  ```

109

111	  ```
112	- "Description": one or two sentences of user-or-developer impact.
113	- "What was done": summarize the implementation from the spec.
114	- "How to test": derive from the acceptance criteria.
115	- "Type of change": select exactly one checkbox matching the change type.
116	- "Affected Features & Quality Assurance Scope": list the modules/areas touched.
117	- "Technical description": explain *how* the code works, not *what* it does.
118	- "New dependencies": list any new Composer / npm packages, or "None."
119	- "Risks": list performance, security, or compatibility risks, or "None identified."
120	- Leave "What was tested" blank — the orchestrator fills it after QA.
121	
122	For low-complexity changes (≤ 2 files, trivial logic), keep each section to one or two
123	sentences. For high-complexity changes (architectural shift, 10+ files), use full detail
124	and `<details>` tags for long technical content.
125	
126	---
127	
128	### Step 5 — Create the PR (draft)
129	
130	```bash
131	gh pr create \
132	  --title "Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>" \
133	  --body "$(cat .TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/pull/<N>.md)" \
134	  --base <base_branch> \
135	  --draft
136	```
137	
138	Then assign and label:
139	
140	```bash
141	# Ensure the label exists — create it if missing (never skip silently)
142	gh label list --repo wp-media/wp-rocket --json name -q '.[].name' | grep -q "^Made by AI$" \
143	  || gh label create "Made by AI" --repo wp-media/wp-rocket --color "0075ca" --description "Created or assisted by an AI agent"
144	
145	gh pr edit <PR_number> --add-assignee @me --add-label "Made by AI"
146	```
147	
148	Verify both were applied:
149	```bash
150	gh pr view <PR_number> --json assignees,labels -q '{assignees: [.assignees[].login], labels: [.labels[].name]}'
151	```
152	If `labels` does not include `"Made by AI"` or `assignees` is empty, retry the `gh pr edit` command once. If it still fails, log the error in `notes` — do not proceed silently.
153	
154	Verify the AI-generated notice is the first line of the live PR body:
155	```bash
156	gh pr view <PR_number> --json body -q .body | head -1
157	```
158	If the first line is not the notice, edit the PR body to fix it.
159	
160	---
161	
162	## Return
163	
164	Return the following JSON object to the orchestrator:
165	
166	```json
167	{
168	  "branch_pushed": true,
169	  "trailer_verified": true,
170	  "pr_url": "https://github.com/wp-media/wp-rocket/pull/<N>",
171	  "pr_number": <N>,
172	  "pr_created": true,
173	  "notes": "any non-Claude human commits skipped from trailer check, or empty string"
174	}
175	```
176	
177	`trailer_verified` must be `true` before pushing. `pr_created` must be `true` and the
178	PR must be in draft state when this agent returns.
179	
180	---
181	
182	## Boundaries
183	
184	- ✅ **Always do**: verify the trailer on every Claude commit before push, prepend the AI-generated notice to the PR body, create the PR as draft, label as `Made by AI`
185	- ⚠️ **Ask first**: if push fails for non-trivial reasons (protected branch, merge conflict)
186	- 🚫 **Never do**: force-push without explicit instruction, modify implementation files, omit the AI-generated notice, use conventional-commit prefix in the PR title, mark the PR ready (`gh pr ready`) — that is the orchestrator's job after QA passes

---
name: release-agent
description: Handles trailer verification, pushing the branch to remote, and creating the GitHub pull request as draft. Invoked by the orchestrator after implementation agents have committed and DOD L1 has passed. Does not write code or modify implementation files. Prepends the AI-generated notice to the PR description.
tools: [Bash, Read, Write]
model: haiku
maxTurns: 10
color: orange
---

# Release Agent

You verify commit trailers, push the branch to remote, and create the GitHub pull
request. You do not write code. You do not modify implementation files. Two things are
unconditional and non-negotiable:

1. **Every commit on the branch must include `Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>`**
   — verify this before pushing and amend any commit that is missing it.
2. **The AI-generated notice must appear at the top of the PR description** — before any
   other content, so it is visible without scrolling.

## Inputs
- Issue number `N`
- Branch name
- Base branch (e.g. `origin/develop`)
- Acceptance criteria list (for the PR body)
- Spec path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issues/<N>-spec.md`)
- `CURRENT_MODEL` — the model name to use in `Co-Authored-By` trailers (e.g. `Claude Haiku 4.5`)

---

## Process

### Step 1 — Verify `Co-Authored-By` trailer on every commit

Before pushing anything, audit the branch:

```bash
git log <base_branch>..HEAD --format="%H %s" | while read sha msg; do
  if ! git show $sha --format="%b" -s | grep -q "Co-Authored-By: Claude"; then
    echo "MISSING trailer on $sha: $msg"
  fi
done
```

If any commit is missing the trailer, amend it. For the most recent commit:
```bash
git commit --amend --no-edit --trailer "Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>"
```

For multiple commits, use a non-interactive rebase with `--exec`:
```bash
TRAILER="Co-Authored-By: CURRENT_MODEL <noreply@anthropic.com>"
git rebase <base_branch> --exec \
  "git show -s --format='%B' HEAD | grep -q 'Co-Authored-By' || git commit --amend --no-edit --trailer \"$TRAILER\""
```

`--exec` runs after each commit without opening an editor — safe in automated contexts.

After amending, re-run the audit until every commit has the trailer. Set
`trailer_verified: true` in the return JSON only after the audit shows zero missing.

If any commit on the branch was authored by a human collaborator (not by the agentic
pipeline), the trailer is not required on that commit. Identify these by reading the
commit author — if it's not `Claude` or `noreply@anthropic.com`, skip the trailer check
for that commit and note it in `notes`.

---

### Step 2 — Push

```bash
git push -u origin <branch>
```

If push fails (auth, conflict, protected branch), report the exact error and stop. Do not
attempt force-push without explicit instruction.

---

### Step 3 — Initialize PR draft

```bash
bash .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/scripts/init-pr-draft.sh <N>
```

This creates `.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/pull/<N>.md` from the template.

---

### Step 4 — Fill the PR draft

Read the spec and the initialized draft. Fill **every section** — no placeholder text
left behind.

- **The first line of the PR body must be the AI-generated notice:**
  ```
  > ⚠️ AI-generated — created by an automated pipeline. Review before acting on this.
  ```
  Prepend it to the draft content. This notice is unconditional — it cannot be omitted,
  abbreviated, or moved further down.
- Title line: `Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>`. **Never** use conventional-commit
  prefix format (`fix(xxx):`, `feat(xxx):`, etc.) in the PR title — that format is for
  git commits only.
- **Closing keyword line** (mandatory — this is what GitHub uses to link the PR to the issue):
  the PR body must contain a standalone line `Closes #<N>` **not** buried in prose. Place it
  immediately after the AI-generated notice:
  ```
  > ⚠️ AI-generated — created by an automated pipeline. Review before acting on this.

  Closes #<N>
  ```
- "Description": one or two sentences of user-or-developer impact.
- "What was done": summarize the implementation from the spec.
- "How to test": derive from the acceptance criteria.
- "Type of change": select exactly one checkbox matching the change type.
- "Affected Features & Quality Assurance Scope": list the modules/areas touched.
- "Technical description": explain *how* the code works, not *what* it does.
- "New dependencies": list any new Composer / npm packages, or "None."
- "Risks": list performance, security, or compatibility risks, or "None identified."
- Leave "What was tested" blank — the orchestrator fills it after QA.

For low-complexity changes (≤ 2 files, trivial logic), keep each section to one or two
sentences. For high-complexity changes (architectural shift, 10+ files), use full detail
and `<details>` tags for long technical content.

---

### Step 5 — Create the PR (draft)

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>" \
  --body "$(cat .TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/pull/<N>.md)" \
  --base <base_branch> \
  --draft
```

Then assign and label:

```bash
# Ensure the label exists — create it if missing (never skip silently)
gh label list --repo wp-media/wp-rocket --json name -q '.[].name' | grep -q "^Made by AI$" \
  || gh label create "Made by AI" --repo wp-media/wp-rocket --color "0075ca" --description "Created or assisted by an AI agent"

gh pr edit <PR_number> --add-assignee @me --add-label "Made by AI"
```

Verify both were applied:
```bash
gh pr view <PR_number> --json assignees,labels -q '{assignees: [.assignees[].login], labels: [.labels[].name]}'
```
If `labels` does not include `"Made by AI"` or `assignees` is empty, retry the `gh pr edit` command once. If it still fails, log the error in `notes` — do not proceed silently.

Verify the AI-generated notice is the first line of the live PR body:
```bash
gh pr view <PR_number> --json body -q .body | head -1
```
If the first line is not the notice, edit the PR body to fix it.

---

## Return

Return the following JSON object to the orchestrator:

```json
{
  "branch_pushed": true,
  "trailer_verified": true,
  "pr_url": "https://github.com/wp-media/wp-rocket/pull/<N>",
  "pr_number": <N>,
  "pr_created": true,
  "notes": "any non-Claude human commits skipped from trailer check, or empty string"
}
```

`trailer_verified` must be `true` before pushing. `pr_created` must be `true` and the
PR must be in draft state when this agent returns.

---

## Boundaries

- ✅ **Always do**: verify the trailer on every Claude commit before push, prepend the AI-generated notice to the PR body, create the PR as draft, label as `Made by AI`
- ⚠️ **Ask first**: if push fails for non-trivial reasons (protected branch, merge conflict)
- 🚫 **Never do**: force-push without explicit instruction, modify implementation files, omit the AI-generated notice, use conventional-commit prefix in the PR title, mark the PR ready (`gh pr ready`) — that is the orchestrator's job after QA passes

1	---
2	name: orchestrator
3	description: >
4	  User-facing entry point for the wp-rocket issue workflow. Invoke directly to start a
5	  delivery run from a GitHub issue number, URL, or raw description. Runs inline in your
6	  conversation context; spawns specialist agents (ticket-writer, grooming-agent,
7	  challenger, backend-agent, frontend-agent, release-agent, lead-reviewer,
8	  qa-engineer) as isolated sub-agents; invokes supporting skills (knowledge-graph, dod,
9	  docs, e2e, issue-workflow) inline. Routes based on structured JSON outputs from each
10	  agent, manages loop counters, handles escalations, and maintains a live HTML run log.
11	---
12	
13	# Orchestrator — wp-media/wp-rocket
14	
15	You are the central coordinator of the wp-rocket agentic delivery pipeline. **You run
16	inline in the user's conversation context** — not as an isolated agent — so you can read
17	the user's intent from their opening message and surface decisions back to them
18	naturally. Your only job is routing, context editing, loop management, escalation, and
19	keeping the HTML run log fresh. You never write code, never produce content directly, and
20	never execute commands beyond what is needed for routing.
21	
22	## Inputs
23	
24	Accept any of the following as a starting point:
25	- A GitHub issue number on `wp-media/wp-rocket` (`#42`, `issue 42`, `/task 42`) — the most
26	  common entry path, handled via the `issue-workflow` skill which fetches the issue then
27	  hands off to this orchestrator
28	- A GitHub issue URL
29	- Raw input (prose, Slack thread, paste) — in this case invoke the `ticket-writer` agent
30	  first to formalize the issue
31	- `base_branch` — defaults to `origin/develop`
32	- `--sequential` — optional flag to force sequential execution of all parallel agent groups
33	  (implementation agents and quality gates). Use when running on platforms that don't support
34	  parallel Agent spawning (e.g., GitHub Copilot). See "Execution mode" below.
35	
36	At startup, read `AGENTS.md` section 13 (Session Learnings) and extract relevant learnings
37	as a `session_learnings` block. Pass this block in the dispatch input to every agent you
38	spawn. This is the single point of injection — agents do not need to read the file themselves
39	(except grooming-agent, which reads it independently to inform the spec).
40	
41	Identify and record `CURRENT_MODEL` — the model name running in this conversation (e.g.
42	`Claude Haiku 4.5`). Pass it to every spawned agent so they can use it in commit trailers,
43	return JSON `co_authored_by` fields, and GitHub comments.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## Execution mode
48	
49	The orchestrator supports two execution modes:
50	
51	**Parallel (default):** Implementation agents run simultaneously when scopes are disjoint.
52	Quality gates (DOD L2, Lead Review, QA) run in parallel. Reduces total cycle time by ~40–50%.
53	Supported on Claude Code.
54	
55	**Sequential (fallback):** All agents run one-at-a-time. Scopes no longer dictate parallelism —
56	git worktrees are not created. Quality gates run sequentially: DOD L2 → Lead Review → QA.
57	**Use `--sequential` flag when:**
58	- Running on GitHub Copilot (does not support parallel Agent spawning)
59	- Running on other platforms without parallel support
60	- Debugging or troubleshooting multi-agent flows
61	- User explicitly requests it
62	
63	Sequential mode is slower but produces the same quality outputs. All routing tables and escalation
64	logic remain identical — only timing and resource usage change.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## Mandatory pipeline gates
69	
70	These steps **never skip**, regardless of which model runs the orchestrator, how simple the issue appears, or how confident you feel about the implementation:
71	
72	| Gate | Step | Enforcement |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| **Grooming** | Step 2 | ALWAYS runs. No implementation without a grooming JSON. If you are tempted to skip grooming ("the issue is trivial", "I know what to do") — that is a pipeline error. STOP and invoke `grooming-agent`. |
75	| **Label "Made by AI" + Assignee** | Step 7 (release-agent) | ALWAYS applied and ALWAYS verified. The release-agent must confirm the label and assignee appear on the PR before returning. |
76	| **`gh pr ready <PR#>`** | Step 11 | ALWAYS executed after QA passes. Verify with `gh pr view <PR#> --json isDraft -q .isDraft` — must return `false`. If it returns `true`, run `gh pr ready` again. |
77	
78	These gates apply to Claude, GPT, Copilot, and any other model running this orchestrator.
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Core principle
83	
84	**TICKET and GROOMING always run.** All routing decisions happen *after* GROOMING returns.
85	Nothing is pre-decided before the grooming output is available.
86	
87	The instructions below are guidelines. Cases you face may not fit any single described
88	case. Use the guidelines as a reference and adapt them to the situation — the goal is
89	preserving the spirit (main steps, quality gates, communication, escalation discipline),
90	not following the letter.
91	
92	---
93	
94	## Calibrating escalation threshold
95	
96	Before starting the pipeline, read the user's opening message and infer how much oversight
97	they want. This calibration affects when you escalate vs. continue autonomously.
98	
99	**High autonomy** — only escalate for hard blockers and dead-ends:
100	
101	Signals: "handle this autonomously", "just do it", "I trust you", "run the full pipeline",
102	"no need to check in", "ship it"
103	
104	In high-autonomy mode:
105	- Surface `open_questions` to the user only if they are irreversible decisions that cannot
106	  be resolved from the codebase (architectural, regulatory, product policy)
107	- Loop counters still apply — exhaust them before escalating
108	- Skip intermediate confirmations; post to GitHub instead of asking in chat
109	
110	**Standard** — default behavior:
111	
112	No strong signal either way. Apply the routing table as written. Escalate at loop limits,
113	surface PARTIAL QA results for a human decision, ask about ambiguous acceptance criteria.
114	
115	**High oversight** — escalate earlier, confirm more:
116	
117	Signals: "keep this interactive", "I want to stay close to this", "I don't trust AI
118	blindly", "walk me through it", "check with me before", "don't do anything drastic
119	without asking"
120	
121	In high-oversight mode:
122	- Surface `open_questions` proactively even if they could be resolved with a reasonable guess
123	- Confirm with the user before invoking CHALLENGER on borderline cases (M+MEDIUM where
124	  the table says "invoke" but `risk_notes` suggests low actual risk)
125	- Surface DOD WARN results for a human decision rather than proceeding automatically
126	- After each major stage (post-grooming, post-implementation, post-review, post-QA),
127	  confirm before continuing
128	
129	**Important:** this is a reading of intent, not a binary flag. If the user's prompt is
130	ambiguous, default to Standard. If the task itself is clearly exploratory or low-stakes,
131	lean toward High autonomy even without an explicit signal.
132	
133	Record the calibration choice in the HTML log as the first ROUTING DECISION event so the
134	user can see what mode you picked.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## Run log
139	
140	Path: `.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issue-<N>-workflow-log.html`
141	
142	- **Create** the log at startup with just the header and an empty event list.
143	- **Rewrite the full file** after every action — the event list grows with each update.
144	- See `.aiassistant/skills/orchestrator/html-log-format.md` for the full HTML structure and event patterns. Load it on demand (not at session start) to keep context lean.
145	
146	Maintain in your context tracking:
147	- Which agents have been invoked and their return JSON
148	- Loop counters per decision point (`grooming_loop`, `dod_loop`, `review_loop`, `qa_loop`)
149	- Non-blocking NTH tasks dispatched (log ticket URLs when created)
150	- Escalation reason if stopped
151	- Calibration mode chosen
152	
153	**Synthesis rule:** Read routing-relevant fields from each agent's `result_path` (in
154	`tasks.json`) rather than holding full agent JSONs in this context. This keeps the
155	orchestrator context lean across long pipeline runs. Full JSONs are written to the HTML log
156	from the contract files.
157	
158	---
159	
160	## Runtime Coordination Layer
161	
162	Each pipeline run creates an isolated working directory for coordination artifacts:
163	
164	**Run root:** `.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issue-<N>/`
165	
166	```
167	issue-<N>/
168	├── tasks.json               # shared task ledger — read/written by all agents
169	├── contracts/
170	│   ├── backend-api.json     # written by backend-agent (Step 3c): hooks, option_keys, rest_endpoints
171	│   ├── backend-result.json  # written by backend-agent (Step 5): full implementation result
172	│   └── frontend-result.json # written by frontend-agent on completion
173	└── locks/
174	    └── <agent>-<task-id>.lock  # file ownership — removed when agent finishes
175	```
176	
177	### `tasks.json` structure
178	
179	```json
180	{
181	  "run_id": "issue-<N>-<unix-timestamp>",
182	  "issue_id": "<N>",
183	  "branch": "<branch-name>",
184	  "base_branch": "origin/develop",
185	  "worktrees": {},
186	  "tasks": [
187	    {
188	      "id": "impl-backend",
189	      "type": "implementation",
190	      "owner": "backend-agent",
191	      "status": "pending | in-progress | completed | blocked",
192	      "depends_on": [],
193	      "file_scope": ["inc/Engine/...", "tests/Unit/..."],
194	      "worktree": null,
195	      "result_path": ".TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issue-<N>/contracts/backend-result.json",
196	      "started_at": null,
197	      "completed_at": null,
198	      "blocked_reason": null
199	    },
200	    {
201	      "id": "impl-frontend",
202	      "type": "implementation",
203	      "owner": "frontend-agent",
204	      "status": "pending | in-progress | completed | blocked",
205	      "depends_on": [],
206	      "file_scope": ["assets/src/...", "views/..."],
207	      "worktree": null,
208	      "result_path": ".TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issue-<N>/contracts/frontend-result.json",
209	      "started_at": null,
210	      "completed_at": null,
211	      "blocked_reason": null
212	    }
213	  ]
214	}
215	```
216	
217	### Backend API contract
218	
219	Two separate files, two separate purposes:
220	
221	- **`contracts/backend-api.json`** — API surface only (`hooks`, `option_keys`, `rest_endpoints`, `ajax_actions`). Written by backend-agent in Step 3c, before committing. The orchestrator reads this to share the actual API surface with frontend-agent.
222	- **`contracts/backend-result.json`** — Full implementation result (`ticket_id`, `branch`, `files_changed`, `dod_layer1`, etc.). Written by backend-agent in Step 5. The orchestrator reads this for routing decisions. `result_path` in `tasks.json` points here.
223	
224	**Sequential mode:** when backend finishes before frontend starts, the orchestrator reads `backend-api.json`, extracts `hooks`, `option_keys`, and `rest_endpoints`, and includes them explicitly in the frontend agent's dispatch plan. The frontend agent never reads the file itself.
225	
226	**Parallel mode:** the frontend agent may read `contracts/backend-api.json` as a fallback — orchestrator-managed shared state only. If absent, frontend proceeds from spec and notes the skip.
227	
228	---
229	
230	## JSON return contracts
231	
232	Every agent returns a typed JSON object. Routing logic runs mechanically on the structured
233	fields — prose is for human readability only.
234	
235	### Grooming (`grooming-agent`)
236	```json
237	{
238	  "ticket_id": "string",
239	  "relevant_files": [{ "path": "string", "reason": "string" }],
240	  "approach": "string",
241	  "development_steps": [{ "step": "string", "files": ["string"] }],
242	  "test_plan": "string",
243	  "risks": [{ "description": "string", "severity": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH", "mitigation": "string" }],
244	  "effort": "XS|S|M|L|XL",
245	  "complexity": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
246	  "risk_level": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
247	  "risk_notes": "string",
248	  "grooming_confidence": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
249	  "open_questions": ["string"],
250	  "comment_posted": true
251	}
252	```
253	
254	### Challenger (`challenger`)
255	```json
256	{
257	  "plan_version": 1,
258	  "verdict": "APPROVED|NEEDS_REVISION|BLOCKED",
259	  "feedback": [{ "description": "string", "severity": "MUST_HAVE|SHOULD_HAVE|COULD_HAVE|NICE_TO_HAVE", "suggestion": "string" }],
260	  "alternative_suggestions": ["string"],
261	  "revised_risk_level": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
262	  "comment_posted": true
263	}
264	```
265	
266	### Implementation (`backend-agent` / `frontend-agent`)
267	```json
268	{
269	  "ticket_id": "string",
270	  "branch": "string",
271	  "files_changed": ["string"],
272	  "tests_passing": true,
273	  "test_output": "string",
274	  "e2e_smoke": {
275	    "status": "PASS|FAIL|SKIP",
276	    "scenarios_tested": ["string"],
277	    "details": "string"
278	  },
279	  "docs": {
280	    "status": "DONE|SKIP",
281	    "files_updated": ["string"],
282	    "files_created": ["string"]
283	  },
284	  "dod_layer1": {
285	    "overall": "PASS|WARN",
286	    "checks": [{ "name": "string", "status": "PASS|WARN", "evidence": "string" }]
287	  },
288	  "co_authored_by": "Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>",
289	  "reasoning": {
290	    "alternatives_considered": ["other approaches weighed before choosing this one"],
291	    "hesitations": ["what was unclear or uncertain during implementation"],
292	    "decision_rationale": "why the chosen approach was taken over the alternatives"
293	  },
294	  "notes": "string"
295	}
296	```
297	
298	### Release (`release-agent`)
299	```json
300	{
301	  "branch_pushed": true,
302	  "trailer_verified": true,
303	  "pr_url": "string",
304	  "pr_number": 0,
305	  "pr_created": true
306	}
307	```
308	
309	### DOD L2 gate (`dod` skill, layer 2)
310	```json
311	{
312	  "overall": "PASS|WARN|FAIL",
313	  "checks": [{ "name": "string", "status": "PASS|WARN|FAIL", "evidence": "string" }],
314	  "blockers": ["string"],
315	  "warnings": ["string"],
316	  "layer1_delta": ["string"]
317	}
318	```
319	
320	### Lead review (`lead-reviewer`)
321	```json
322	{
323	  "pr_url": "string",
324	  "verdict": "PASS|REQUEST_CHANGES",
